newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin braces for strikes, Yeltsin foes win polls.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin braces for strikes, Yeltsin foes win polls.

text.p: Russian nationalists and communists celebrated big victories on Monday in three local elections, serving President Boris Yeltsin notice of deep discontent with the Kremlin before a day of strikes.

In a sign of the disillusionment over unpaid wages and pensions Vasily Starodubtsev, one of the leaders of a hardline coup attempt against Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev in 1991, was among the winners in Sunday's three local polls.

Yeltsin has promised to end the wage delays and promoted young liberal reformers to do so in a still incomplete government reshuffle. Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said on Monday the bulk of the changes would be completed this week.

"The country is in an exceptionally difficult situation -- it may be the most difficult since 1991," said Yevgeny Yasin, who lost his post of economy minister last week but is expected to maintain a strong informal influence.
"We should act and act quickly," he told a news conference. "To resume economic growth we will have to take some unpopular measures connected with reducing the budget deficit."

Chernomyrdin admitted federal and local authorities, and especially employers, had done "far from everything" to ensure workers received wages on time and promised the government would take "the most drastic measures" to sort out delays.
But the question hanging over reformers was whether Russians, for years fed rosy pictures about their bright future around the corner, would believe yet another promise.

The new government will face its first test on Thursday, when trade unions plan to hold a day of nationwide protests over chronic delays in wages and pensions, which the organisers say will involve millions of people in strikes and protest rallies.
The outcome of local polls held on the weekend gave Yeltsin another reminder that many Russians have turned their hearts against reforms and that their patience is running out.
Itar-Tass news agency said communist-backed Starodubtsev won 60 percent of the votes in an election for governor of Tula, south of Moscow, and secured a seat in parliament's upper house.
Starodubtsev was a member of the eight-man committee of hardliners who tried to overthrow Gorbachev in 1991 and failed because of defiance led by Yeltsin.

Communist Anatoly Belonogov scored a similar easy victory for the governorship of the Amur region bordering China, and nationalist Dmitry Rogozin won a seat in the lower house of parliament in an election in the southern region of Voronezh.
Rogozin is head of the nationalist Congress of Russian Communities which has cooperated closely with General Alexander Lebed, an outspoken Yeltsin opponent.

Yeltsin, 66, who just returned from a summit in Helsinki with U.S. President Bill Clinton, will briefly turn his attention away from the economy and reshuffle to meet Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda on Tuesday. He arrived on Monday.

Also this week, Yeltsin is expected to meet Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen. Quan, too, flew in on Monday. Russia is turning its eyes eastward at a time of strain with the West over NATO's plans to take in new members from the former Soviet bloc.

Apart from opposition to NATO enlargement there is only one other area of agreement between Yeltsin and his conservative opponents -- the need to re-integrate with its western neighbour, the ex-Soviet republic of Belarus.
Yeltsin and Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko are due to meet for new talks on integration in Moscow on April 2 -- the first anniversary of a treaty setting up a two-way "community".
The Kremlin said the Belarus hardline leader's crackdown on a pro-independence demonstration in capital Minsk on the weekend was an internal matter which would not change integration plans.
